The comparison requires testing the same option in different choice sets while holding price, quality, and decision goals constant; an intermediate option may also genuinely be best for the person's needs.

A midpriced camera becomes more popular after an expensive premium camera is added. The example fits if the new premium option changes the midpriced camera's choice share without changing its features or the buyer's requirements. A cheap camera added at the other boundary can also alter the reference frame. Countering the effect means returning to absolute constraints—budget, required capability, durability, and acceptable tradeoffs—rather than treating the menu's middle as evidence of optimality. Menu position is a relational cue, not a measurement of fit.

examples.text: A midpriced camera becomes more popular after an expensive premium model is added to the display.
examples.note: The midpriced camera has not improved; its relative position now offers a psychologically comfortable middle between two extremes.

counters: Define must-have requirements and budget limits before viewing the available set, then score each option against those criteria.
Ask whether removing or adding an irrelevant alternative would change the choice and compare the option's absolute tradeoffs.
limitations: An intermediate option can genuinely offer the best balance, and choice-set context can contain useful information about quality or service.
Observed share changes can reflect menu prominence, price anchoring, or demand segmentation rather than compromise alone.
biases.evidenceNote: Context effects in multi-option choice are repeatedly observed, but compromise magnitudes vary with attribute ranges, decision difficulty, expertise, and the construction of the choice set.

biases.name: Confirmation bias
biases.summary: Seeking, interpreting, or remembering evidence in ways that favor an existing belief.
biases.body:
Confirmation bias is seeking, interpreting, or remembering information in ways that favor an existing belief. It can operate through selective search, unequal standards for evidence, biased interpretation of ambiguous results, or better memory for supporting examples. The comparison is between how a favored and disfavored hypothesis are tested under the same rules, not between accepting strong evidence and accepting weak evidence.

After deciding that a supplement works, a buyer may read positive reviews closely while dismissing negative reviews as unreliable without applying the same criteria. The example fits when the evaluation rule changes with the review's direction and when the buyer avoids evidence that could distinguish the hypotheses. A fair test may still produce an asymmetric conclusion if evidence quality is genuinely asymmetric. Precommitting disconfirming observations, using blinded coding, and recording search endpoints make the standard visible before motivated interpretation begins. The search process matters even when the favored conclusion happens to be true.

examples.text: After deciding a supplement works, a buyer accepts positive reviews and dismisses negative reviews without applying the same quality criteria.
examples.note: The direction of the evidence changes the rule used to judge it, which is the relevant distortion rather than the buyer's final belief alone.

counters: State what result would change the conclusion, search for it deliberately, and apply a preregistered quality rule to both directions of evidence.
Use blinded analysis or independent reviewers when coding ambiguous observations that could support either hypothesis.
limitations: Rejecting weak contrary evidence is appropriate when the same quality standard is applied consistently and stronger evidence supports the favored claim.
A belief can be correct despite confirmation-biased reasoning, so outcome agreement does not remove the process concern.
biases.evidenceNote: Selective information search and interpretation are robust findings, but observed effects depend on motivation, accountability, evidence quality, and whether the task permits a clear disconfirmation.

biases.name: Congruence bias
biases.summary: Testing a preferred hypothesis without seeking observations that distinguish it from alternatives.
biases.body:
Congruence bias is testing a preferred hypothesis only with observations that it predicts, without seeking results that would distinguish it from alternatives. A confirming observation can feel decisive even when competing explanations predict the same observation. The comparison is between a merely compatible test and a discriminating test whose possible outcomes have different implications for the hypotheses.

To test whether a plant needs sunlight, a person moves it into sunlight without comparing water, temperature, or a control plant. Growth supports the sunlight hypothesis only weakly because many explanations predict growth after the move. A test that varies sunlight while holding water and temperature stable, with a shaded comparison, creates more informative contrasts. Congruence is not a flaw in every positive test: if alternatives make different predictions under the observed condition, confirmation can be discriminating. Compatibility is weaker evidence than a result that an alternative could not predict. A shared prediction is not a unique prediction.

examples.text: To test whether a plant needs sunlight, you move it into sunlight without controlling water, temperature, or another plant.
examples.note: The observed improvement is compatible with several explanations, so the test cannot tell sunlight apart from the uncontrolled changes.

counters: List the leading alternatives and choose an observation for which they make different predictions.
Use controls, counterexamples, or interventions that vary the suspected cause while holding plausible co-causes stable.
limitations: A congruent test is informative when competing hypotheses genuinely predict different outcomes under that test.
Perfect discrimination is often impossible, so evidence can accumulate through several partially informative tests rather than one decisive experiment.
biases.evidenceNote: The preference for confirmatory tests is a recurring reasoning error, but its practical impact depends on whether the alternatives were represented and whether tests are chosen adaptively.

biases.name: Conservatism bias in belief revision
biases.summary: Revising a belief too little in response to informative new evidence.
biases.body:
Conservatism bias in belief revision is changing a belief too little after receiving evidence that should materially alter the odds. An initial estimate remains overly influential because the new evidence is discounted, treated as redundant without justification, or translated into an insufficient probability change. The comparison is between the actual revision and an update based on the evidence's reliability and dependence, not between a large update and any cautious attitude.

A forecaster barely lowers demand after several independent indicators show a major contraction. The example fits if the indicators are genuinely informative, measured well, and not simply repeated versions of one source. A small update is appropriate when evidence is weak, dependent, noisy, or generated by a process known to change. Recording a prior, likelihood assumptions, and dependence between signals makes under-updating visible and prevents a vague preference for stability from masquerading as calibration. The update should reflect information, not merely preserve continuity.

examples.text: A forecaster barely lowers a demand estimate after several independent indicators show a major contraction.
examples.note: If the indicators are independent and predictive, retaining the old estimate reflects excessive inertia rather than justified caution about one weak signal.

counters: State the prior, expected reliability, and dependence of each signal, then calculate or narrate the direction and size of a reasonable update.
Review forecasts against later outcomes and distinguish poor updating from evidence that was genuinely uninformative at the time.
limitations: Caution is rational when evidence is correlated, noisy, selected after the fact, or generated by a changed measurement process.
Formal Bayesian updating still depends on a model; numerical precision can conceal rather than solve uncertainty about likelihoods.
biases.evidenceNote: Under-revision is a common finding in belief-updating tasks, but robustness varies with feedback, incentives, domain expertise, probability format, and evidence dependence.

biases.name: Consistency bias
biases.summary: Reconstructing past attitudes or beliefs as more similar to current ones than they actually were.
biases.body:
Consistency bias reconstructs past attitudes, beliefs, or preferences as more similar to current ones than they actually were. The present self provides an organizing narrative of continuity, while changes of mind are harder to retrieve unless dated records preserve them. The comparison is between current recollection and contemporaneous statements or behavior, not between memory and a presumption that people should have changed.

A person remembers always supporting a policy despite an old letter opposing it. The example fits if the letter is contemporaneous evidence and the later memory assimilates the earlier position to the current one. This differs from choice-supportive bias, which favors the option chosen after a decision, and from change bias, which exaggerates the amount of difference between states. Stable attitudes can be real; the existence of agreement across time is not itself proof of reconstruction. Dated notes make genuine continuity and genuine change equally discoverable. Continuity is a hypothesis about the past, not a privilege of present identity.

examples.text: You remember always supporting a policy despite an old dated letter opposing it.
examples.note: The record supplies direct evidence of an earlier attitude, while current recollection has been smoothed into a story of personal continuity.

counters: Use dated statements, versions, and contemporaneous decisions when reconstructing how a view developed.
Ask separately what the person believed then, what changed, and what evidence supports the current account rather than forcing a single continuous narrative.
limitations: People can maintain stable attitudes, and a discrepancy with one record may reflect context, wording, or a temporary exception.
Recollection and records can both be incomplete, so the diagnosis should preserve uncertainty about the earlier state.
biases.evidenceNote: Consistency in autobiographical recall is a documented reconstruction tendency, but its magnitude depends on identity, delay, importance of the attitude, and availability of dated records.

biases.name: Continued influence effect
biases.summary: Using corrected misinformation in later reasoning even after acknowledging the correction.
biases.body: Using corrected misinformation in later reasoning even after acknowledging the correction. A correction may change explicit belief without removing the misinformation's role in an explanation. The inaccurate detail remains available when the person reconstructs what happened, especially if no supported alternative account replaces it.

examples.text: A report first blames a warehouse fire on stored chemicals, then corrects that detail. Later you explain the fire's spread by referring to the chemicals anyway.

counters: State what is known after the correction and build an explanation that does not depend on the withdrawn detail.
limitations: Remembering that a false report occurred is not the same as using its contents as factual support.

biases.name: Contrast effect
biases.summary: Judging an item differently because it is compared with a recently encountered item.
biases.body: Judging an item differently because it is compared with a recently encountered item. The comparison context can shift a rating without changing the target's attributes.

examples.text: A moderately priced meal seems cheap immediately after viewing a much more expensive menu.

counters: Use a stable reference set and compare the target under more than one presentation order.
limitations: A relevant comparison can improve judgment when it matches the actual choice set.

biases.name: Courtesy bias
biases.summary: Giving an agreeable or favorable response to avoid offending the person requesting it.
biases.body: Giving an agreeable or favorable response to avoid offending the person requesting it. Interpersonal politeness can conceal dissatisfaction in interviews or feedback.

examples.text: A guest praises a meal to the host but rates it poorly on an anonymous questionnaire.

counters: Offer private, neutral channels for feedback and normalize criticism.
limitations: A favorable answer can be sincere; anonymity is not a guarantee of accuracy.

biases.name: Coverage bias
biases.summary: Distorting a population estimate because the sampling frame leaves out relevant parts of that population.
biases.body: Distorting a population estimate because the sampling frame leaves out relevant parts of that population. People outside the frame have no chance, or an inadequate chance, of appearing in the sample.

examples.text: An internet-only poll estimates preferences of all residents while excluding residents without internet access.

counters: Compare the sampling frame with the target population and address excluded groups.
limitations: Restricting a frame is legitimate when the target population is explicitly restricted in the same way.

biases.name: Cryptomnesia
biases.summary: Remembering an idea while failing to recognize that it came from an earlier source.
biases.body: Remembering an idea while failing to recognize that it came from an earlier source. The content feels newly generated because its origin is not retrieved.

examples.text: A songwriter sincerely believes a recalled melody is an original composition.

counters: Check prior exposure and keep source notes while developing ideas.
limitations: Independent discovery of a similar idea can occur without forgotten exposure.

biases.name: Decoy effect
biases.summary: Changing preference between two options after adding a third option dominated by one of them.
biases.body: Changing preference between two options after adding a third option dominated by one of them. The inferior decoy makes its dominating neighbor appear more attractive by comparison.

examples.text: A small subscription and a large subscription attract equal interest until an overpriced medium plan boosts sales of the large plan.

counters: Compare the original options without the dominated alternative.
limitations: A new option can legitimately change a decision when it adds relevant information or constraints.

biases.name: Default effect
biases.summary: Choosing an option more often because it is preselected or applies without active intervention.
biases.body: Choosing an option more often because it is preselected or applies without active intervention. Inertia, perceived endorsement, and switching effort can each contribute.

examples.text: Employees remain in a preset retirement contribution plan without comparing available rates.

counters: Review the default against personal objectives and make an active selection.
limitations: A well-chosen default can serve the user's interests and reduce decision costs.

biases.name: Defensive attribution
biases.summary: Explaining harm in ways that protect one's belief in personal safety or distance oneself from the victim.
biases.body: Explaining harm in ways that protect one's belief in personal safety or distance oneself from the victim. Perceived similarity and perceived avoidability can affect assignments of blame.

examples.text: A driver blames an accident victim's character to sustain the belief that careful people like herself are safe.

counters: Separate evidence about responsibility from the desire to feel protected.
limitations: An attribution of responsibility may be justified by documented conduct and circumstances.

biases.name: Denomination effect
biases.summary: Spending equivalent amounts differently depending on whether money is held in large or small denominations.
biases.body: Spending equivalent amounts differently depending on whether money is held in large or small denominations. Breaking a large note can feel more consequential than spending several small notes of the same total value.

examples.text: A shopper keeps one fifty-dollar note but spends five ten-dollar notes.

counters: Track total expenditure independently of the denominations used.
limitations: Transaction costs or change availability can make denominations practically relevant.

biases.name: Denominator neglect
biases.summary: Judging frequency, risk, or success from a numerator while neglecting the relevant total.
biases.body: Judging frequency, risk, or success from a numerator while neglecting the relevant total. A large count can seem impressive even when it represents a small proportion.

examples.text: A treatment's ten recoveries are praised without noting that one thousand people received it.

counters: State the total population and calculate comparable proportions.
limitations: Counts remain relevant when total burden rather than individual probability is the question.

biases.name: Detection bias
biases.summary: Creating systematic differences in measured outcomes through unequal methods of outcome assessment.
biases.body: Creating systematic differences in measured outcomes through unequal methods of outcome assessment. Assessors' knowledge or different surveillance procedures can change what gets recorded.

examples.text: An unblinded evaluator searches more intensively for side effects in one trial group.

counters: Use comparable assessment procedures and blind assessors where feasible.
limitations: A measured difference may remain real after differences in detection are addressed.

biases.name: Disposition effect
biases.summary: Selling investments that have gained value too readily while holding losing investments too long.
biases.body: Selling investments that have gained value too readily while holding losing investments too long. The purchase price can become a psychological reference point that displaces expected future performance.

examples.text: An investor sells a promising winner to lock in a gain but keeps a failing stock to avoid realizing a loss.

counters: Compare expected future returns and risks without treating the purchase price as a target.
limitations: Tax rules, transaction costs, and portfolio needs can justify different sale decisions.

biases.name: Distinction bias
biases.summary: Overweighting differences between options when comparing them together that matter less when experiencing one alone.
biases.body: Overweighting differences between options when comparing them together that matter less when experiencing one alone. Joint evaluation can highlight small attributes that are hard to notice in ordinary use.

examples.text: A buyer pays much more for a screen difference visible side by side but imperceptible at home.

counters: Evaluate each option separately under realistic use conditions.
limitations: Side-by-side differences matter when the task actually requires precise discrimination.

biases.name: Diversification bias
biases.summary: Choosing excessive variety when selecting several future consumptions at once compared with choosing them separately.
biases.body: Choosing excessive variety when selecting several future consumptions at once compared with choosing them separately. Simultaneous selection can exaggerate the value of variety over repeated enjoyment of a favorite.

examples.text: A student orders a different snack for every week in advance but chooses the same favorite when deciding weekly.

counters: Consider the preference likely to apply at each consumption time.
limitations: Variety can rationally hedge uncertain tastes or changing availability.

biases.name: Dread aversion
biases.summary: Preferring to bring forward an unpleasant event to reduce the burden of anticipating it.
biases.body: Preferring to bring forward an unpleasant event to reduce the burden of anticipating it. Waiting can add disutility beyond the unpleasant event itself.

examples.text: A person chooses an earlier painful appointment to stop spending weeks anticipating it.

counters: Separate the event's consequences from the costs of waiting and anticipation.
limitations: Reducing genuine anticipatory distress can be a coherent preference rather than an error.

biases.name: Duration neglect
biases.summary: Giving an episode's length too little weight when evaluating its total pleasantness or unpleasantness.
biases.body: Giving an episode's length too little weight when evaluating its total pleasantness or unpleasantness. Retrospective ratings may depend more on salient moments and endings than elapsed duration.

examples.text: A longer uncomfortable procedure is rated better because its final minutes are milder.

counters: Record duration and moment-by-moment experience when total burden matters.
limitations: Duration can be irrelevant when the question concerns peak intensity or the ending itself.

biases.name: Ecological sampling bias
biases.summary: Distorting inference because the locations, times, or situations sampled do not represent the environment of interest.
biases.body: Distorting inference because the locations, times, or situations sampled do not represent the environment of interest. This broad label concerns the match between observation settings and the ecological target.

examples.text: A wildlife survey samples only roadside habitats and generalizes to an entire forest.

counters: Sample across relevant habitats and times according to the intended population.
limitations: A roadside sample is appropriate when the target is specifically roadside wildlife.

biases.name: Effort justification
biases.summary: Valuing an outcome more highly because obtaining it required substantial effort or sacrifice.
biases.body: Valuing an outcome more highly because obtaining it required substantial effort or sacrifice. Positive evaluation can reduce tension between the cost endured and the outcome received.

examples.text: A club member insists a mediocre group is exceptional after enduring a difficult initiation.

counters: Assess the outcome using standards set before the effort was spent.
limitations: Effort can genuinely develop skill, attachment, or enjoyment that increases value.

biases.name: Egocentric bias
biases.summary: Giving one's own perspective or contribution excessive weight relative to other people's.
biases.body: Giving one's own perspective or contribution excessive weight relative to other people's. Access to one's own experiences can make them seem disproportionately central.

examples.text: Each coauthor estimates having completed most of a shared project.

counters: Compare contribution estimates with shared records and independent accounts.
limitations: A person can actually contribute more; unequal estimates need evidential assessment.

biases.name: Egocentric memory bias
biases.summary: Remembering shared events in ways that exaggerate one's own role or contribution.
biases.body: Remembering shared events in ways that exaggerate one's own role or contribution. Readily retrieved personal actions may crowd out other participants' less accessible actions.

examples.text: Years after a team success, a member remembers generating nearly every important idea.

counters: Use contemporaneous notes and other participants' accounts.
limitations: Clear records of a major personal contribution can support an unequal attribution.

biases.name: Empathy gap
biases.summary: Underestimating how a different emotional or bodily state will affect preferences or behavior.
biases.body: Underestimating how a different emotional or bodily state will affect preferences or behavior. A person in a calm or satiated state may poorly anticipate decisions made under anger, pain, or hunger.

examples.text: After lunch, someone plans to skip dinner easily and is surprised by intense evening hunger.

counters: Make plans using evidence from past behavior in the relevant state.
limitations: Preferences may remain stable across states, and prediction errors are not inevitable.

biases.name: Endowment effect
biases.summary: Valuing an item more highly when owning it than when considering acquiring the same item.
biases.body: Valuing an item more highly when owning it than when considering acquiring the same item. Ownership can change reference points and the perceived cost of giving something up.

examples.text: A person will pay ten dollars for a mug but demands thirty dollars to sell it once assigned ownership.

counters: Compare buy and sell decisions using the same alternatives and information.
limitations: Transaction costs, attachment, and information differences can create legitimate valuation gaps.

biases.name: Escalation of commitment
biases.summary: Investing further resources in a failing course partly because resources have already been committed.
biases.body: Investing further resources in a failing course partly because resources have already been committed. Protecting an earlier decision can displace comparison of future costs and benefits.

examples.text: A firm keeps funding an unviable project to avoid admitting its earlier investment was wasted.

counters: Evaluate only future consequences and establish independent stopping criteria.
limitations: Continuing is justified when expected future benefits exceed future costs.

biases.name: Essentialism bias
biases.summary: Treating a category as if all members share a deep, fixed essence that explains their traits.
biases.body: Treating a category as if all members share a deep, fixed essence that explains their traits. This psychological tendency can encourage rigid generalizations about social or biological groups.

examples.text: A child assumes an adopted animal must behave exactly like its birth category regardless of upbringing.

counters: Examine within-category variation and the processes that produce the trait.
limitations: Some categories track stable causal structures, but their existence does not justify every essentialist inference.

biases.name: Exaggerated expectation
biases.summary: Forming an extreme forecast from limited or selectively salient evidence.
biases.body: Forming an extreme forecast from limited or selectively salient evidence. This is a broad, less standardized label rather than one sharply defined cognitive effect.

examples.text: After one record sales week, a retailer forecasts record sales every week of the coming year.

counters: Compare the forecast with base rates and uncertainty ranges.
limitations: An extreme forecast can be justified by strong evidence of a sustained structural change.

biases.name: Experimenter expectancy effect
biases.summary: Allowing a researcher's expectations to influence participants' behavior, measurement, or interpretation.
biases.body: Allowing a researcher's expectations to influence participants' behavior, measurement, or interpretation. Subtle cues and flexible observations can transmit a preferred outcome without deliberate fraud.

examples.text: A researcher gives more encouragement to participants expected to perform well.

counters: Standardize instructions and blind relevant researchers to conditions or hypotheses.
limitations: An observed effect is not evidence of expectancy influence without a plausible pathway and supporting data.

biases.name: Extension neglect
biases.summary: Giving too little weight to how many cases or objects a judgment covers.
biases.body: Giving too little weight to how many cases or objects a judgment covers. A rating based on a vivid exemplar may remain nearly unchanged when the set grows substantially.

examples.text: A donor offers almost the same amount to save two thousand birds as to save two hundred thousand birds.

counters: Make the size of the affected set explicit and compare marginal outcomes.
limitations: Value need not grow linearly with count when resources, saturation, or other values matter.

biases.name: Extremeness aversion
biases.summary: Avoiding options at the extremes of a choice set because of their relative position.
biases.body: Avoiding options at the extremes of a choice set because of their relative position. The available range can influence preferences even when an option's own attributes stay fixed.

examples.text: A diner avoids a wine mainly because it is the most expensive bottle on the menu.

counters: Compare each option with actual preferences and budget independently of rank.
limitations: An extreme price can provide relevant information about financial burden.

biases.name: Extrinsic incentives bias
biases.summary: Expecting other people to be more driven by external rewards than oneself.
biases.body: Expecting other people to be more driven by external rewards than oneself. People may emphasize purpose in explaining their own choices but money in explaining others' choices.

examples.text: A manager says she works for meaningful impact while assuming colleagues care only about bonuses.

counters: Ask about others' motives and compare behavior under equivalent conditions.
limitations: Some people are primarily motivated by financial incentives in particular contexts.

biases.name: Fading affect bias
biases.summary: Finding that negative emotional reactions to remembered events fade faster than positive reactions.
biases.body: Finding that negative emotional reactions to remembered events fade faster than positive reactions. The label concerns the affect attached to autobiographical memories, not necessarily loss of factual detail.

examples.text: An old holiday's stressful delays lose their sting while its enjoyable moments remain emotionally vivid.

counters: Use records made at the time when evaluating the original experience.
limitations: Trauma and other conditions can produce different emotional memory patterns.

biases.name: False consensus effect
biases.summary: Overestimating how widely other people share one's beliefs, preferences, or behavior.
biases.body: Overestimating how widely other people share one's beliefs, preferences, or behavior. One's social circle and personal choice can be mistaken for a representative sample.

examples.text: A cyclist assumes almost everyone supports a road proposal because all her cycling friends do.

counters: Seek representative data beyond your immediate network.
limitations: A belief may actually be widespread; prevalence requires evidence.

biases.name: False memory
biases.summary: Recalling an event or detail that did not occur or occurred differently.
biases.body: Recalling an event or detail that did not occur or occurred differently. Memory reconstructs experiences and can incorporate inference, suggestion, or material from another source.

examples.text: A witness remembers a stop sign at an intersection that actually had a yield sign.

counters: Compare independent contemporaneous evidence without leading the witness.
limitations: Vividness and confidence alone establish neither accuracy nor falsity.

biases.name: False uniqueness effect
biases.summary: Underestimating how widely other people share one's desirable qualities or choices.
biases.body: Underestimating how widely other people share one's desirable qualities or choices. A positive trait may feel unusually distinctive when comparable behavior in others is not visible.

examples.text: A volunteer assumes very few peers donate time despite a survey showing volunteering is common.

counters: Compare self-assessment with representative information about others.
limitations: A trait can truly be rare; the issue is an inaccurate prevalence estimate.

biases.name: Favoritism
biases.summary: Giving preferential treatment on the basis of a personal relationship rather than relevant merit or rules.
biases.body: Giving preferential treatment on the basis of a personal relationship rather than relevant merit or rules. A decision may serve affiliation while being presented as an impartial evaluation.

examples.text: A supervisor awards a contract to a friend despite a better qualified competing bid.

counters: Use documented criteria and independent assessment when relationships create conflicts.
limitations: A relationship can be relevant when trust or established performance is explicitly part of the task.

biases.name: Focusing effect
biases.summary: Overweighting the aspect of a situation currently receiving attention.
biases.body: Overweighting the aspect of a situation currently receiving attention. A salient feature can dominate predictions of satisfaction while other contributors are neglected.

examples.text: A house buyer predicts lasting happiness from a sea view while overlooking a long daily commute.

counters: Evaluate the whole pattern of daily consequences using a consistent checklist.
limitations: A focused feature may actually dominate utility in a particular decision.

biases.name: Framing effect
biases.summary: Changing a judgment or choice when equivalent information is described differently.
biases.body: Changing a judgment or choice when equivalent information is described differently. A gain or loss description can change evaluation without changing the underlying outcomes.

examples.text: A treatment described as ninety percent survival attracts more support than the same treatment described as ten percent mortality.

counters: Restate the information in equivalent gain and loss terms before choosing.
limitations: Descriptions that communicate different facts are not equivalent frames.

biases.name: Frequency illusion
biases.summary: Feeling that something has become more common after newly noticing or learning about it.
biases.body: Feeling that something has become more common after newly noticing or learning about it. Increased attention and easier recognition can mimic a change in prevalence.

examples.text: After learning a new word, you notice it several times and conclude its use suddenly increased.

counters: Compare dated frequency data instead of relying on newly heightened attention.
limitations: A real increase in exposure can occur alongside increased attention.

biases.name: Functional fixedness
biases.summary: Failing to consider uses of an object beyond its familiar function.
biases.body: Failing to consider uses of an object beyond its familiar function. A learned purpose can constrain the search for a solution.

examples.text: Someone needing a doorstop overlooks a heavy book because books are for reading.

counters: List the object's physical properties separately from its customary purpose.
limitations: A customary use may remain the safest or most effective use.

biases.name: Fundamental attribution error
biases.summary: Overweighting personal dispositions and underweighting situational constraints when explaining another person's conduct.
biases.body: Overweighting personal dispositions and underweighting situational constraints when explaining another person's conduct. An observed action may reveal less about stable character than the observer assumes.

examples.text: A customer calls a cashier unfriendly without accounting for a mandatory script and an exhausting shift.

counters: Identify constraints and compare the person's behavior across situations.
limitations: Repeated behavior across varied circumstances can support a dispositional explanation.

biases.name: Funding bias
biases.summary: A tendency for research choices or conclusions to favor the interests of the funding source.
biases.body: A tendency for research choices or conclusions to favor the interests of the funding source. Study questions, comparators, publication decisions, and interpretation can all be affected.

examples.text: A sponsor tests its product only against an unusually weak competing treatment and advertises superiority.

counters: Inspect funding disclosures, comparator choices, preregistration, and independent replications.
limitations: Sponsorship alone does not show that a particular result is false.

biases.name: Gender bias
biases.summary: Systematic judgment or treatment influenced by gender when it is irrelevant or given unjustified weight.
biases.body: Systematic judgment or treatment influenced by gender when it is irrelevant or given unjustified weight. Stereotypes can affect expectations, opportunity, and interpretation of identical behavior.

examples.text: Identical assertive conduct is praised as leadership in one applicant and penalized as abrasiveness in another because of gender.

counters: Use behavior-based criteria and audit equivalent cases for unequal treatment.
limitations: A gender-related distinction requires assessment of its relevance rather than automatic acceptance or rejection.

biases.name: Group attribution error
biases.summary: Inferring individual group members' views from a group outcome or a judgment about the group.
biases.body: Inferring individual group members' views from a group outcome or a judgment about the group. Collective decisions do not necessarily reveal what each member privately believes.

examples.text: A resident assumes every council member supported a policy because the council adopted it by majority vote.

counters: Check individual positions and the decision rule that produced the collective result.
limitations: A recorded unanimous individual vote provides stronger evidence than group membership alone.

biases.name: Group polarization
biases.summary: Moving toward a more extreme version of a group's initial tendency after discussion.
biases.body: Moving toward a more extreme version of a group's initial tendency after discussion. Shared arguments and social comparison can shift the collective position.

examples.text: A mildly risk-seeking committee endorses a much riskier plan after members reinforce one another's optimistic reasons.

counters: Collect independent judgments and introduce substantive contrary evidence before deliberation.
limitations: Discussion can justifiably produce stronger views when it supplies strong new evidence.

biases.name: Halo effect
biases.summary: Allowing a favorable overall impression or one positive trait to improve judgments of unrelated traits.
biases.body: Allowing a favorable overall impression or one positive trait to improve judgments of unrelated traits. The evaluator may infer several virtues from evidence for only one.

examples.text: An articulate applicant is rated highly for numerical accuracy without any arithmetic assessment.

counters: Assess each relevant trait with separate evidence.
limitations: Some traits correlate, but the strength and relevance of that relationship need support.

biases.name: Hard–easy effect
biases.summary: Showing different confidence calibration across difficult and easy tasks, often overconfidence on hard tasks and underconfidence on easy ones.
biases.body: Showing different confidence calibration across difficult and easy tasks, often overconfidence on hard tasks and underconfidence on easy ones. The observed pattern depends partly on task selection, measurement, and statistical effects.

examples.text: A quiz taker assigns high confidence to difficult answers that are frequently wrong but understates accuracy on very easy questions.

counters: Compare confidence with actual accuracy separately by difficulty using enough observations.
limitations: A single hard error or easy success does not establish a calibration pattern.

biases.name: Hedonic forecasting error
biases.summary: Misjudging how pleasant or unpleasant a future experience will feel.
biases.body: Misjudging how pleasant or unpleasant a future experience will feel. Forecasts can neglect adaptation, competing experiences, or the difference between imagined and lived circumstances.

examples.text: Someone predicts a promotion will keep them delighted every day for years.

counters: Use experiences of comparable people and your own past adaptation as reference points.
limitations: Some events produce sustained changes in well-being; adaptation is not universal.

biases.name: Herding bias
biases.summary: Following others' choices more than independent information or incentives warrant.
biases.body: Following others' choices more than independent information or incentives warrant. Imitation can amplify a shared mistake when people infer that earlier choosers must know more.

examples.text: Traders copy a buying wave despite private evidence that the asset is overpriced.

counters: Distinguish independent evidence from observations that merely repeat the same signal.
limitations: Following others can be rational when their actions reveal reliable private information.

biases.name: Hindsight bias
biases.summary: Overestimating how predictable an outcome was after learning what happened.
biases.body: Overestimating how predictable an outcome was after learning what happened. Outcome knowledge can obscure the alternatives that were plausible beforehand.

examples.text: After an unexpected election result, an analyst says the winner was obviously inevitable.

counters: Compare the claim with forecasts recorded before the outcome.
limitations: A genuinely accurate advance forecast is evidence of foresight rather than hindsight bias.

biases.name: Hindsight memory distortion
biases.summary: Remembering one's earlier prediction as closer to the outcome than it actually was.
biases.body: Remembering one's earlier prediction as closer to the outcome than it actually was. This is the memory-specific form of hindsight bias.

examples.text: A forecaster recalls predicting a fall in prices despite a dated note predicting a rise.

counters: Preserve timestamped predictions and confidence estimates.
limitations: Changing an opinion after new evidence is different from misremembering the earlier opinion.

biases.name: Historical bias in datasets
biases.summary: Reproducing historical inequities through data that accurately record an unequal world.
biases.body: Reproducing historical inequities through data that accurately record an unequal world. A model can perpetuate exclusion even when the recorded observations are not measurement mistakes.

examples.text: A recruitment model trained on past promotions learns that a historically excluded group rarely becomes a manager.

counters: Assess whether the historical target and resulting decisions match the intended objective.
limitations: Accurate historical description does not by itself justify using the same pattern to allocate future opportunities.

biases.name: Horn effect
biases.summary: Letting one unfavorable impression lower judgments of other, unsupported traits.
biases.body: Letting one unfavorable impression lower judgments of other, unsupported traits. A negative cue may spill into evaluations that need independent evidence.

examples.text: An applicant's untidy clothes lead an interviewer to assume poor programming ability without a work sample.

counters: Rate job-relevant skills independently of unrelated negative impressions.
limitations: A negative cue can be relevant when it directly concerns a defined performance requirement.

biases.name: Hostile attribution bias
biases.summary: Interpreting ambiguous conduct as deliberately hostile.
biases.body: Interpreting ambiguous conduct as deliberately hostile. Unclear intent is resolved toward threat or malice rather than remaining uncertain.

examples.text: A delayed reply is taken as an intentional insult despite plausible workload or delivery problems.

counters: Compare hostile and benign explanations with evidence about intent.
limitations: Documented threats or repeated targeted conduct can justify a hostile interpretation.

biases.name: Hostile media effect
biases.summary: Perceiving a news account as biased against one's own side, sometimes when opposing partisans both make that judgment.
biases.body: Perceiving a news account as biased against one's own side, sometimes when opposing partisans both make that judgment. Prior commitments can influence which wording and omissions seem unfair.

examples.text: Supporters of opposing teams each judge the same match report as favoring the other team.

counters: Evaluate specific factual errors and selection choices against an explicit standard.
limitations: A report can actually be biased; partisan disagreement alone proves neither neutrality nor unfairness.

biases.name: Hot-hand bias
biases.summary: Inferring that a recent success streak makes further success more likely without adequate evidence of a changing success probability.
biases.body: Inferring that a recent success streak makes further success more likely without adequate evidence of a changing success probability. Real performance dependence can exist, so a streak is not automatically illusory.

examples.text: A bettor predicts another win solely because a roulette player has won three independent spins.

counters: Check whether the process is independent and whether predictive persistence is established.
limitations: A genuine improvement, learning effect, or persistent performance state can make recent success informative.

biases.name: Hyperbolic discounting
biases.summary: Discounting delayed rewards especially steeply over short delays, allowing preferences to reverse as rewards approach.
biases.body: Discounting delayed rewards especially steeply over short delays, allowing preferences to reverse as rewards approach. The relative attraction of sooner and later rewards can depend on how close they are to the present.

examples.text: You prefer 110 dollars in thirty-one days to 100 in thirty days, but prefer 100 today to 110 tomorrow.

counters: Choose commitment rules while comparing options from a consistent time perspective.
limitations: Delay costs, liquidity needs, and uncertainty can justify some preference for earlier rewards.

biases.name: Identifiable-victim effect
biases.summary: Responding more strongly to a particular identified sufferer than to comparable statistical victims.
biases.body: Responding more strongly to a particular identified sufferer than to comparable statistical victims. A name or story can make one person's need more vivid than an equally serious anonymous need.

examples.text: A donor gives more to a named child's treatment than to an equally effective fund helping several unnamed children.

counters: Compare impact, severity, and effectiveness alongside the personal story.
limitations: A specific relationship or obligation can legitimately justify helping an identified person.

biases.name: IKEA effect
biases.summary: Valuing a product more because one helped make or assemble it.
biases.body: Valuing a product more because one helped make or assemble it. Personal labor can increase attachment and the perceived value of the result.

examples.text: Someone prices their self-assembled shelf above a comparable professionally assembled shelf.

counters: Compare independent quality and market alternatives before setting value.
limitations: Enjoyment of creating something can be a real benefit distinct from market value.

biases.name: Illusion of asymmetric insight
biases.summary: Believing one understands other people better than they understand oneself.
biases.body: Believing one understands other people better than they understand oneself. Private access to one's own complexity can make others seem more transparent and simpler.

examples.text: A colleague claims to know exactly why you disagreed while insisting you cannot understand her motives.

counters: Seek the other person's account and separate observation from inferred motives.
limitations: Unequal access to information can sometimes create a real difference in understanding.

biases.name: Illusion of competence
biases.summary: Mistaking familiar or easy-to-process material for knowledge that can be recalled or applied independently.
biases.body: Mistaking familiar or easy-to-process material for knowledge that can be recalled or applied independently. Rereading can create recognition without the ability to reconstruct an explanation. Smooth processing is then used as a substitute for a performance test, inflating the learner's estimate of mastery.

examples.text: You recognize every worked solution while reading a chapter, but cannot solve a similar problem after closing the book.

counters: Test delayed recall and solve new problems without looking at the explanation.
limitations: Fluent performance supported by successful independent testing can reflect genuine mastery.

biases.name: Illusion of control
biases.summary: Overestimating one's influence over outcomes governed substantially by chance or outside forces.
biases.body: Overestimating one's influence over outcomes governed substantially by chance or outside forces. Choosing, participating, or using a ritual can feel causal without changing the odds.

examples.text: A lottery buyer believes choosing the numbers makes the ticket more likely to win.

counters: Compare outcomes when the supposed control is present and absent.
limitations: Skill-dependent tasks can provide real control even when their outcomes also involve luck.

biases.name: Illusion of explanatory depth
biases.summary: Overestimating how well one understands a mechanism until required to explain it in detail.
biases.body: Overestimating how well one understands a mechanism until required to explain it in detail. Familiarity with an object or label can be mistaken for knowledge of its causal workings.

examples.text: Someone claims to understand a zipper but cannot explain how its teeth lock and release.

counters: Write or draw the complete mechanism and identify missing steps.
limitations: Knowing how to use something does not require understanding every part of its mechanism.

biases.name: Illusion of external agency
biases.summary: Attributing one's own action or outcome to an external agent when that attribution is unsupported.
biases.body: Attributing one's own action or outcome to an external agent when that attribution is unsupported. This broad label concerns mistaken authorship or influence and should not be inferred solely from an unusual report.

examples.text: A person believes a lucky charm guided their hand to a winning card despite no evidence of influence.

counters: Identify the actual action pathway and test the alleged external contribution.
limitations: External influence can be real; unfamiliar subjective experiences alone do not identify their cause.

biases.name: Illusion of transparency
biases.summary: Overestimating how clearly others can detect one's internal feelings or intentions.
biases.body: Overestimating how clearly others can detect one's internal feelings or intentions. A vivid private experience can feel more publicly visible than it is.

examples.text: A nervous speaker assumes the whole audience can hear anxiety that listeners barely notice.

counters: Compare the predicted visibility with independent observer reports.
limitations: Some emotions do produce conspicuous behavioral cues.

biases.name: Illusion of understanding
biases.summary: Overestimating how completely an account explains an event or system.
biases.body: Overestimating how completely an account explains an event or system. A coherent narrative can feel like a complete causal explanation even when important mechanisms and alternatives are missing. Predicting outcomes or explaining intermediate steps can reveal gaps that a polished retrospective story conceals.

examples.text: After reading a short account of a market crash, you believe you can predict the next crash but cannot specify a testable mechanism or timing conditions.

counters: State the mechanism, competing explanations, and an observation that would discriminate between them.
limitations: Understanding can be partial and useful without supporting precise prediction of a complex system.

biases.name: Illusion of validity
biases.summary: Feeling unwarrantedly confident in a judgment because the available information forms a coherent story.
biases.body: Feeling unwarrantedly confident in a judgment because the available information forms a coherent story. Internal consistency can be mistaken for predictive accuracy even when evidence is limited or redundant.

examples.text: An interviewer becomes certain of future success after hearing a polished, coherent career narrative with no performance data.

counters: Check predictive accuracy on independent outcomes and seek conflicting evidence.
limitations: Coherence supported by independent, discriminating evidence can strengthen a judgment.

biases.name: Illusory correlation
biases.summary: Perceiving an association that is absent or stronger than the data support.
biases.body: Perceiving an association that is absent or stronger than the data support. Distinctive or emotionally salient co-occurrences can be easier to remember than ordinary combinations.

examples.text: A person notices two crimes involving a minority group and concludes membership strongly predicts crime without comparing rates.

counters: Tabulate all relevant combinations and use appropriate denominators.
limitations: A suspected association may be real, but memorable examples alone cannot establish its size.

biases.name: Illusory self–other similarity
biases.summary: Perceiving another person as more similar to oneself than evidence warrants.
biases.body: Perceiving another person as more similar to oneself than evidence warrants. This overlaps assumed similarity and social projection rather than naming a wholly separate mechanism.

examples.text: A traveler assumes a new acquaintance shares their dietary and political preferences because they share one hobby.

counters: Check the relevant preference directly instead of extrapolating from one shared feature.
limitations: Independent evidence of shared preferences can justify a similarity judgment.

biases.name: Illusory superiority
biases.summary: Rating one's abilities or desirable traits above other people's more than the evidence warrants.
biases.body: Rating one's abilities or desirable traits above other people's more than the evidence warrants. Comparative self-assessments can be favorable even when objective performance is ordinary.

examples.text: Most members of a team each estimate being among its top few performers without checking results.

counters: Use defined performance measures and comparable reference groups.
limitations: Many people can exceed a skewed population mean; above-average claims are not automatically contradictory.

biases.name: Illusory truth effect
biases.summary: Rating a statement as more credible after repeated exposure even without additional supporting evidence.
biases.body: Rating a statement as more credible after repeated exposure even without additional supporting evidence. Familiarity and easier processing can be mistaken for independent confirmation.

examples.text: A repeated rumor starts to feel true despite every repetition tracing back to the same unverified post.

counters: Track original evidence and count independent sources rather than repetitions.
limitations: Repetition can accompany genuine corroboration; source independence and quality matter.

biases.name: Imagination inflation
biases.summary: Becoming more confident that an event occurred after imagining it.
biases.body: Becoming more confident that an event occurred after imagining it. Imagined detail can later be mistaken for evidence from an actual experience.

examples.text: After repeatedly imagining breaking a window as a child, an adult becomes less sure the event was only imagined.

counters: Distinguish records of imagining from independent evidence that the event happened.
limitations: An imagined event can resemble a real event without establishing or disproving its occurrence.

biases.name: Impact bias
biases.summary: Overestimating the intensity or duration of one's emotional response to a future event.
biases.body: Overestimating the intensity or duration of one's emotional response to a future event. Forecasts may focus on the event while neglecting adaptation and other parts of daily life.

examples.text: An applicant expects a rejection to make every day miserable for a year but recovers much sooner.

counters: Compare predictions with prior recovery and the experiences of similar people.
limitations: Some losses produce lasting distress; rapid adaptation is not assured.

biases.name: In-group bias
biases.summary: Favoring members of one's own group over comparable outsiders.
biases.body: Favoring members of one's own group over comparable outsiders. Shared identity can influence trust, resource allocation, and evaluation independently of individual merit.

examples.text: A panel gives an equally qualified applicant from its own club a higher rating.

counters: Apply explicit criteria and compare equivalent cases with group cues concealed where practical.
limitations: A real obligation to a group can justify some differential treatment without supporting every preference.

biases.name: Information bias
biases.summary: Seeking information that cannot improve the decision being made.
biases.body: Seeking information that cannot improve the decision being made. This decision-making sense differs from information bias in epidemiology, which concerns systematic measurement error.

examples.text: A buyer orders an expensive test after confirming that every possible result leads to the same action.

counters: State which possible result would change the action before collecting more information.
limitations: Information can have value for future decisions, learning, or accountability even when it does not change the immediate choice.

biases.name: Insensitivity to sample size
biases.summary: Failing to account for the greater variability of estimates from smaller samples.
biases.body: Failing to account for the greater variability of estimates from smaller samples. A small sample can produce extreme proportions more readily than a large one from the same population.

examples.text: Someone expects a small clinic and a large hospital to be equally likely to report a day with eighty percent male births.

counters: Compare sampling variability using the actual sample sizes.
limitations: Small samples can be useful, but their uncertainty must be represented.

biases.name: Insensitivity to scope
biases.summary: Responding too little to the scale of a benefit, harm, or affected population.
biases.body: Responding too little to the scale of a benefit, harm, or affected population. This is a scope-focused form of extension neglect and often concerns valuations or willingness to contribute.

examples.text: A person offers almost the same donation to protect one hundred endangered animals as to protect ten thousand otherwise comparable animals.

counters: Compare outcomes at several explicitly stated scales.
limitations: Diminishing marginal value and resource limits can justify some less-than-proportional response.

biases.name: Intentionality bias
biases.summary: Interpreting actions or outcomes as intended more readily than evidence of intention warrants.
biases.body: Interpreting actions or outcomes as intended more readily than evidence of intention warrants. Knowledge of an outcome, its moral character, or the action's appearance can influence inferred intent.

examples.text: A spilled drink is judged a deliberate slight before considering that the tray was unstable.

counters: Distinguish intention, foresight, negligence, and accident using evidence about the actor's plans.
limitations: A deliberate action can have unintended consequences; these are separate judgments.

biases.name: Intergroup attribution bias
biases.summary: Explaining similar conduct differently according to the actor's group membership.
biases.body: Explaining similar conduct differently according to the actor's group membership. Positive in-group conduct may be credited to character while positive out-group conduct is explained away by circumstances.

examples.text: A fan calls their team's fair play good character but calls identical conduct by rivals a publicity tactic.

counters: Compare explanations for matched conduct with group identities reversed.
limitations: Different circumstances can justify different explanations when supported by evidence.

biases.name: Interviewer bias
biases.summary: Influencing responses or their interpretation through an interviewer's wording, behavior, expectations, or recording decisions.
biases.body: Influencing responses or their interpretation through an interviewer's wording, behavior, expectations, or recording decisions. A leading prompt can create an apparent attitude or recollection rather than merely measure it.

examples.text: An interviewer asks whether a clearly irresponsible policy angered the respondent.

counters: Use neutral standardized prompts and check recordings against coded responses.
limitations: Clarifying an answer is legitimate when the clarification does not supply the desired response.

biases.name: Irrational escalation
biases.summary: Continuing a failing action because of prior investment despite worse expected future results.
biases.body: Continuing a failing action because of prior investment despite worse expected future results. This overlaps escalation of commitment and emphasizes persistence that current costs and benefits do not justify.

examples.text: A gambler doubles a losing wager to recover earlier losses even though the game remains unfavorable.

counters: Compare future options without requiring recovery of sunk costs.
limitations: Increasing investment can be rational when new evidence improves expected returns.

biases.name: Just-world bias
biases.summary: Assuming people generally receive outcomes they deserve and adjusting judgments to preserve that belief.
biases.body: Assuming people generally receive outcomes they deserve and adjusting judgments to preserve that belief. Victims may be blamed to make misfortune appear controllable or morally ordered.

examples.text: A bystander assumes a robbery victim must have been careless despite having no evidence about the circumstances.

counters: Separate responsibility evidence from the desire for a fair and predictable world.
limitations: Some outcomes do reflect conduct; the inference requires evidence in the particular case.

biases.name: Language bias
biases.summary: Distorting an evidence review by preferentially locating, including, or interpreting research in selected languages.
biases.body: Distorting an evidence review by preferentially locating, including, or interpreting research in selected languages. Findings published in excluded languages may differ from those in the included record.

examples.text: A review of a treatment includes only English-language reports although relevant trials were published elsewhere.

counters: Search relevant languages and report language restrictions and their likely consequences.
limitations: A language restriction is not proof that the resulting estimate is biased in a particular direction.

biases.name: Law of the instrument
biases.summary: Relying excessively on a familiar tool or method across problems it does not fit.
biases.body: Relying excessively on a familiar tool or method across problems it does not fit. Expertise in one technique can narrow the search for alternative approaches.

examples.text: A statistician insists on a regression model for a problem that first requires defining the measurement correctly.

counters: Specify the problem before choosing the method and compare plausible alternatives.
limitations: A familiar tool can remain appropriate when its assumptions and purpose fit the task.

biases.name: Length-time bias
biases.summary: Overrepresenting slower-progressing conditions because they remain detectable for longer.
biases.body: Overrepresenting slower-progressing conditions because they remain detectable for longer. A screening sample can include a disproportionate share of long-duration cases.

examples.text: Periodic screening finds more slow-growing tumors, making screened cases appear to have better prognosis even without a treatment benefit.

counters: Account for detection windows and compare outcomes with an appropriate study design.
limitations: Longer survival from detection can reflect bias, treatment benefit, or both.

biases.name: Less-is-better effect
biases.summary: Valuing a smaller offering more highly when separate evaluation makes a favorable attribute easier to judge.
biases.body: Valuing a smaller offering more highly when separate evaluation makes a favorable attribute easier to judge. Evaluation mode can produce preference reversals between separate and joint comparison.

examples.text: A full small cup of ice cream is rated more favorably alone than a larger but partly empty cup containing more ice cream.

counters: Compare the absolute quantities and the same options jointly.
limitations: Presentation can affect genuine enjoyment, so the relevant goal must be specified.

biases.name: Linguistic intergroup bias
biases.summary: Describing behavior at different levels of abstraction in ways that sustain group stereotypes.
biases.body: Describing behavior at different levels of abstraction in ways that sustain group stereotypes. Favorable in-group conduct and unfavorable out-group conduct may be framed as stable traits rather than isolated acts.

examples.text: A supporter says our member is generous but their member donated money after identical charitable acts.

counters: Compare descriptions for matched events and separate actions from trait claims.
limitations: Different wording is not evidence of bias when the available behavioral history actually differs.

biases.name: Look-ahead bias
biases.summary: Using information in an analysis or simulation that would not have been available at the decision time.
biases.body: Using information in an analysis or simulation that would not have been available at the decision time. Future knowledge can make a historical strategy appear more successful than it could have been in practice.

examples.text: A trading backtest uses a company's revised earnings before the revision's publication date.

counters: Enforce timestamped data availability and separate training from later evaluation.
limitations: Retrospective explanation can use later information when it is not presented as an achievable advance prediction.

biases.name: Loss aversion
biases.summary: Giving a loss more psychological weight than a comparable gain relative to a reference point.
biases.body: Giving a loss more psychological weight than a comparable gain relative to a reference point. The response concerns changes from a reference level rather than final wealth alone.

examples.text: A person rejects an even chance to gain one hundred dollars or lose one hundred dollars.

counters: Examine the reference point and compare the full final outcomes.
limitations: Risk aversion, financial constraints, or utility curvature can also explain rejection of a gamble.

biases.name: Measurement bias
biases.summary: Systematically recording a variable differently from the quantity or construct it is intended to represent.
biases.body: Systematically recording a variable differently from the quantity or construct it is intended to represent. A biased instrument or procedure can shift estimates even in a large sample.

examples.text: An incorrectly calibrated scale records every participant as two kilograms heavier.

counters: Validate instruments against an appropriate reference and examine group-specific error.
limitations: Random measurement error can reduce precision without producing the same constant directional shift.

biases.name: Memory conformity
biases.summary: Changing one's reported memory toward another person's account.
biases.body: Changing one's reported memory toward another person's account. Discussion can blend witnessed details with information supplied after the event.

examples.text: After talking to a co-witness, someone remembers a red jacket that only the other witness reported.

counters: Collect independent accounts before discussion and record the source of each detail.
limitations: Agreement can reflect accurate independent observation rather than conformity.

biases.name: Mental accounting
biases.summary: Treating resources differently according to psychological accounts rather than their overall economic role.
biases.body: Treating resources differently according to psychological accounts rather than their overall economic role. Money assigned to a bonus, gift, or daily spending category can be treated as less interchangeable than it is.

examples.text: Someone pays high-interest debt slowly while keeping an equal low-interest savings balance labeled vacation money.

counters: Compare the combined budget, opportunity costs, and constraints across accounts.
limitations: Separate budgets can usefully support commitment, planning, and legal obligations.

biases.name: Misattribution of memory
biases.summary: Remembering content while assigning it to the wrong source, person, time, or experience.
biases.body: Remembering content while assigning it to the wrong source, person, time, or experience. The content can be familiar even when its origin is not accurately retrieved.

examples.text: You remember a news claim as coming from a trusted broadcaster although you saw it in an unverified post.

counters: Distinguish familiarity with the claim from evidence about where it came from.
limitations: Uncertainty about a source does not establish that the remembered content is false.

biases.name: Misinformation effect
biases.summary: Allowing misleading information encountered after an event to alter later recollection or reports.
biases.body: Allowing misleading information encountered after an event to alter later recollection or reports. Post-event suggestion can become confused with the original perceptual experience.

examples.text: After a question mentions broken glass, a witness reports seeing glass that was absent from the scene.

counters: Use neutral questions and preserve early independent accounts.
limitations: A changed report may reflect several processes; the label alone does not prove an underlying memory was permanently replaced.

biases.name: Money illusion
biases.summary: Judging financial changes in nominal amounts while neglecting changes in purchasing power.
biases.body: Judging financial changes in nominal amounts while neglecting changes in purchasing power. A larger currency amount can represent less real value when prices rise sufficiently.

examples.text: A worker feels richer after a three percent raise despite prices increasing six percent.

counters: Compare inflation-adjusted income, prices, and debt obligations.
limitations: Nominal amounts remain relevant to fixed contracts and cash-flow constraints.

biases.name: Mood-congruent memory bias
biases.summary: Retrieving or interpreting memories in ways that match one's current mood.
biases.body: Retrieving or interpreting memories in ways that match one's current mood. Current sadness can make unhappy episodes more accessible without reflecting the full history.

examples.text: After a discouraging meeting, someone recalls only earlier workplace failures and judges the whole year a failure.

counters: Review dated records and recall contrasting experiences before making a global assessment.
limitations: Accessible negative memories can be accurate even when their selection is unrepresentative.

biases.name: Moral credential effect
biases.summary: Using an earlier demonstration of moral character as permission or protection for a later questionable choice.
biases.body: Using an earlier demonstration of moral character as permission or protection for a later questionable choice. A prior action may alter how a person interprets subsequent conduct rather than actually justifying it.

examples.text: A manager treats having hired one disadvantaged applicant as proof that a later discriminatory decision cannot be prejudiced.

counters: Evaluate each decision against the same substantive standard.
limitations: A history of fair conduct can be relevant evidence without exempting a particular action from scrutiny.

biases.name: Moral luck bias
biases.summary: Allowing outcomes beyond an actor's control to influence moral blame or praise.
biases.body: Allowing outcomes beyond an actor's control to influence moral blame or praise. The catalog label concerns outcome-sensitive judgment within the broader philosophical debate about moral luck.

examples.text: Two equally reckless drivers receive very different blame because only one happens to encounter a pedestrian.

counters: Assess intention, foreseeable risk, and control separately from the realized harm.
limitations: Outcome-sensitive legal liability or remedial responsibility can differ from an assessment of culpability.

biases.name: Naive cynicism
biases.summary: Assuming other people's judgments are more self-interested than evidence warrants.
biases.body: Assuming other people's judgments are more self-interested than evidence warrants. Observers may discount sincere conviction as a cover for personal advantage.

examples.text: A voter assumes a neighbor's policy preference must be motivated by private financial gain without checking the neighbor's reasons.

counters: Compare stated reasons, incentives, and behavior rather than inferring selfishness automatically.
limitations: Evidence of conflicts of interest can justify skepticism in a specific case.

biases.name: Naive diversification
biases.summary: Dividing resources roughly evenly among available options without assessing the resulting overall allocation.
biases.body: Dividing resources roughly evenly among available options without assessing the resulting overall allocation. The menu's structure can determine the portfolio more than underlying risks or goals.

examples.text: An employee allocates equal amounts to every listed fund and accidentally concentrates most savings in overlapping stock funds.

counters: Evaluate total exposure and desired allocation before dividing money among menu items.
limitations: An equal-weight strategy can be defensible under some uncertainty and cost constraints.

biases.name: Naive realism in social psychology
biases.summary: Treating one's own perspective as an objective view of reality and disagreement as evidence of others' ignorance or bias.
biases.body: Treating one's own perspective as an objective view of reality and disagreement as evidence of others' ignorance or bias. The observer may fail to recognize interpretation in their own perception of a social dispute.

examples.text: Two negotiators each regard their preferred settlement as simply the fair facts and the other's as partisan distortion.

counters: Describe the assumptions and information that lead each side to its conclusion.
limitations: Acknowledging perspective does not imply that every interpretation is equally accurate.

biases.name: Negativity bias
biases.summary: Giving negative information more influence than comparable positive information.
biases.body: Giving negative information more influence than comparable positive information. Bad events can command attention, learning, or evaluation beyond their frequency or relevance.

examples.text: A customer lets one mildly unpleasant interaction outweigh many equally informative positive interactions with a service.

counters: Compare severity, frequency, and diagnostic value rather than valence alone.
limitations: Negative information can be more informative or consequential in some settings.

biases.name: Neglect of probability
biases.summary: Focusing on the nature of a possible outcome while underweighting its likelihood.
biases.body: Focusing on the nature of a possible outcome while underweighting its likelihood. An emotionally vivid consequence can dominate choice even when its probability changes greatly.

examples.text: A traveler pays the same large premium to avoid a frightening risk whether its chance is one in a hundred or one in a million.

counters: Compare the probability, severity, uncertainty, and cost of reducing the risk.
limitations: A low-probability catastrophic outcome can deserve substantial attention when its consequences are large.

biases.name: Nonresponse bias
biases.summary: Distorting a survey estimate because people who do not respond differ relevantly from respondents.
biases.body: Distorting a survey estimate because people who do not respond differ relevantly from respondents. A large respondent count does not remove systematic differences caused by nonresponse.

examples.text: A workplace satisfaction survey looks favorable because the most dissatisfied staff decline to participate.

counters: Compare response patterns and assess plausible outcomes among nonrespondents.
limitations: A low response rate does not establish the direction or magnitude of bias by itself.

biases.name: Normalcy bias
biases.summary: Underestimating or dismissing a serious disruption because familiar conditions are expected to continue.
biases.body: Underestimating or dismissing a serious disruption because familiar conditions are expected to continue. Prior routine can be treated as reassurance despite credible warning signs.

examples.text: Residents ignore a clear evacuation warning because previous storms caused little damage locally.

counters: Use the current warning evidence and predefined response thresholds.
limitations: Maintaining calm is not itself bias, and some warnings are poorly calibrated.

biases.name: Not-invented-here bias
biases.summary: Rejecting an idea or solution because it originated outside one's own team or organization.
biases.body: Rejecting an idea or solution because it originated outside one's own team or organization. Origin can substitute for evaluating fitness, cost, and quality.

examples.text: An engineering team rebuilds a reliable external tool solely because it did not create the original.

counters: Compare internal and external options using the same requirements.
limitations: Security, licensing, support, and integration constraints can justify an internal solution.

biases.name: Observer bias
biases.summary: Letting an observer's expectations influence what they notice, record, or interpret.
biases.body: Letting an observer's expectations influence what they notice, record, or interpret. Ambiguous observations are especially vulnerable when coding rules are flexible.

examples.text: A researcher expects a treatment to work and classifies borderline movements as improvement only in the treatment group.

counters: Use blinded observation, operational definitions, and independent coding.
limitations: Interpretation necessarily involves judgment; bias requires a systematic distortion relative to the intended standard.

biases.name: Omission bias
biases.summary: Judging harmful inaction less harshly than a comparable harmful action without adequate justification.
biases.body: Judging harmful inaction less harshly than a comparable harmful action without adequate justification. Doing nothing can feel less causally or morally responsible even when a relevant duty to act exists.

examples.text: A decision-maker tolerates preventable harm from withholding treatment but rejects an equally risky active treatment solely because it involves acting.
